summary: Lists the state of standardization of Internet protocols as determined by the Internet Architecture Board. It is historic and was replaced by RFC 1920.

eli5.summary: A report card showing which Internet rules are official and which aren't. It was replaced by a later one.

questions: which protocols were internet standards in late 1995
how is an internet protocol standardized
what does it mean for a protocol to be historic
subtitle: A snapshot of protocol standardization status in late 1995

tldr.problem: The Internet community needs a clear, authoritative way to understand which protocols are standards and which are still experimental, draft, or informational.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1880 catalogs all Internet protocols and their standardization status according to their maturity level (standard, draft standard, proposed standard, experimental, informational, or historic) and their requirement level (required, recommended, elective, limited use, or not recommended).
tldr.outcome: This became a periodic publication. RFC 1880 is now historic, replaced by RFC 1920.

today: RFC 1920 replaced this document, which is now historic. RFC 1880 was a periodic snapshot of protocol standards as of November 1995.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 1880 describes the standardization status of protocols used in the Internet as determined by the Internet Architecture Board (IAB). It is intended as a reference document to be issued approximately quarterly.

The document explains the standardization process, defines the terms used to categorize protocols, and provides comprehensive lists of protocols organized by their maturity level and requirement level.
sections.eli5: This document is like a checklist that says which Internet rules have been tested and approved, and which are still being tried out.

sections.title: Understanding Protocol States and Statuses
sections.content:
Protocols are categorized along two independent dimensions. The first is maturity level or STATE: Standard, Draft Standard, Proposed Standard, Experimental, Informational, or Historic. The second is requirement level or STATUS: Required (must be implemented), Recommended (should be implemented), Elective (may or may not be implemented), Limited Use (for specialized circumstances), or Not Recommended (should not be used for general purposes).

A Standard Protocol has been officially established by the IESG and assigned an STD number. A Draft Standard is actively being considered for standardization with substantial testing underway. A Proposed Standard is a candidate for future standardization. Experimental protocols are for research or specific experiments. Informational protocols are from other standards organizations or vendors. Historic protocols have been superseded or are no longer in use.
sections.eli5: Every Internet rule gets two labels. One says how tested it is (from fully approved to just experimental). The other says whether programs must use it, should use it, or can skip it.

sections.title: The Standardization Process
sections.content:
The Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) develops Internet standards through its working groups, overseen by the Internet Engineering Steering Group (IESG). Protocols move through a formal track: they start as Proposed Standards, advance to Draft Standards (after at least 6 months and two independent implementations), and eventually become Standards (after at least 4 months at Draft level and demonstrated interoperability).

The Internet Architecture Board and Internet Research Task Force (IRTF) provide oversight and guidance. The RFC Editor publishes all documents, but standards track documents require IESG approval. Once a protocol becomes a Standard, it is assigned an STD number in addition to its RFC number.
sections.eli5: New Internet rules go through several rounds of testing and approval. They start as ideas, then tests, then get approved step by step. This takes time to make sure the rules actually work.

sections.title: Protocol Categories and Lists
sections.content:
The RFC organizes protocols into sections by maturity level: Standard Protocols, Network-Specific Standard Protocols, Draft Standard Protocols, Proposed Standard Protocols, Experimental Protocols, Informational Protocols, and Historic Protocols. Within the standards track, protocols are further marked with their requirement level (Required, Recommended, or Elective).

Examples of Standard Protocols listed include IP, TCP, UDP, SMTP, FTP, and DNS. The Telnet Options are collected in a separate section with their individual states and statuses. The document notes that protocol status may change between editions, marking such changes with asterisks.
sections.eli5: The document sorts all the rules into groups based on whether they are approved, being tested, or old and not used anymore. It lists hundreds of protocols and says whether each one must be used, can be optional, or should not be used.

sections.title: Related Standards Documents
sections.content: RFC 1880 references several companion documents that provide more detail. These include the Assigned Numbers document (RFC 1700), which lists all protocol-specific parameter values; the Host Requirements documents (RFCs 1122 and 1123), which specify what must be implemented in Internet hosts; and the Gateway Requirements document (RFC 1812), which specifies requirements for routers. The document also notes that DoD MIL-STD specifications for IP and TCP exist, though RFCs 1122 and 1123 take precedence.
sections.eli5: Other documents explain the details of how protocols work and what features must be built in. This document points to where to find those details.
